title: Google to Disable Assistant on Smart Speakers in 2025, Says Verge Report
body:
Google announced a sweeping overhaul of its smart‑home ecosystem that will see the Nest app retired and the Google Home app become the sole hub for managing connected devices. In addition, the company plans to phase out Google Assistant on a range of smart speakers and displays beginning in 2025, shifting users toward newer hardware and a consolidated software experience. The changes mark the most significant restructuring of Google’s consumer‑focused IoT portfolio in years and signal a strategic push to streamline development, improve security, and better compete with rival ecosystems.

The transition will begin with the Nest app, which has served as the primary interface for controlling thermostats, cameras, doorbells, and other Nest‑branded hardware since its launch in 2019. Google says the app will be discontinued in early 2025, with existing users prompted to migrate their devices to the Google Home app. The latter, originally introduced as a companion for Chromecast and Google Nest speakers, has been expanded over the past two years to support a broader array of third‑party products. By consolidating device management under a single platform, Google hopes to reduce fragmentation, simplify updates, and provide a more cohesive user experience across Android, iOS, and web interfaces.

The retirement of Google Assistant on legacy smart speakers is a parallel move aimed at encouraging adoption of newer devices that support the company’s latest voice‑AI capabilities. Google will cease support for the original Google Home, Home Mini, and Home Max models, as well as older Nest Hub and Nest Hub Max units, after a one‑year deprecation window. Users of these devices will still be able to control their smart‑home gadgets via the Google Home app, but voice interactions will be limited to basic commands. Newer hardware, such as the Nest Audio and the latest Nest Hub (2nd gen), will continue to receive full Assistant functionality, including advanced features like multi‑room audio, on‑device processing, and integration with Google’s generative AI tools.

Industry analysts view the shift as a pragmatic response to mounting competition from Amazon’s Alexa ecosystem and Apple’s HomeKit, both of which have long offered unified control apps. “Google’s decision to retire the Nest app and focus on Google Home is about reducing complexity for developers and consumers alike,” says Maya Patel, senior analyst at TechInsights. “It also gives Google a single codebase to push security patches and AI enhancements, which is crucial as privacy concerns grow.” The move could also be motivated by the company’s broader AI strategy, as the Google Home app is now a conduit for Bard‑powered suggestions and contextual automation, features that are harder to retrofit into older Nest‑only interfaces.

Consumers, however, may face short‑term inconvenience. The migration process requires users to log into the Google Home app, re‑authorize each device, and re‑configure routines that were previously stored in the Nest app. Google has pledged a “smooth transition” with in‑app prompts, step‑by‑step guides, and a dedicated support page, but early reports from beta testers indicate occasional hiccups, especially with legacy Nest cameras that rely on older firmware. Moreover, the deprecation of Assistant on older speakers could accelerate hardware turnover, prompting some users to replace functional devices solely to retain full voice‑control capabilities.

From a security standpoint, consolidating control under the Google Home app may allow Google to enforce stricter authentication measures, such as biometric login and end‑to‑end encryption for device commands. The company also plans to roll out a unified “Secure Home” badge for certified devices, mirroring similar programs in the automotive and mobile sectors. This could reassure privacy‑concerned users who have been wary of always‑listening microphones and data collection practices.

Looking ahead, Google’s real test will be how quickly it can migrate its vast installed base—estimated at over 150 million Nest and Google Home devices worldwide—without eroding user confidence. If the transition proceeds smoothly, the unified Google Home platform could become a more powerful hub for AI‑driven automation, positioning Google as a stronger contender in the increasingly crowded smart‑home market. The company’s next steps, including potential integration of generative AI assistants and expanded third‑party partnerships, will shape whether the consolidation translates into tangible benefits for consumers or simply a rebranding of existing services.
